title: TANGO: RNA Topology and Geometry Co-Design
claim: Matching target geometry does not guarantee matching topology; prior methods fall short on one objective while ours clusters in the region satisfying both.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared axes with dashed thresholds and shaded quadrants
description: Three side-by-side scatter plots with identical axes: sc-TM on the x-axis and sc-BP-F1 on the y-axis, each running from 0 to 1. Panel a (gRNAde) uses gray points, panel b (RIDER) uses orange points, and panel c (TANGO) uses blue points. Dashed lines mark thresholds at sc-TM = 0.45 and sc-BP-F1 = 0.5. The upper-right quadrant is shaded light green, meaning both objectives are satisfied. The lower-right quadrant is shaded light red, meaning good geometry but poor topology. Faint density contours sit under the points. A few points have black outlines and fall in the red region. gRNAde points are spread diagonally and many are low. RIDER points cluster near the center and along a diagonal. TANGO points concentrate tightly in the upper-right green region. The eye goes first to the blue cluster in panel c.
caption: RNA 3D inverse design requires joint topology and geometry fidelity. Each point denotes a designed sequence evaluated by fold-back self-consistency, with tertiary-structure fidelity measured by sc-TM and secondary-topology fidelity measured by sc-BP-F1. The upper-right region contains designs that satisfy both objectives. Existing 3D RNA design methods can produce geometry-consistent but topology-inconsistent designs, showing that tertiary similarity alone does not guarantee recovery of the target base-pairing topology. Conversely, topology preservation alone is insufficient for specifying the final tertiary fold.
abstract: Designing RNA sequences that satisfy target tertiary-structure objectives is an important problem in RNA engineering, with broad applications in synthetic biology and therapeutics. Existing 3D RNA design methods have made substantial progress, but they largely treat the target fold as a geometry-only objective. This is incomplete for RNA, whose functional folds are specified not only by tertiary geometry but also by secondary base-pairing topology. We therefore formulate RNA inverse design as a topology-and-geometry co-design problem and propose TANGO, a multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for this task. TANGO adopts a staged curriculum: it first learns a topology-aware policy from secondary-structure targets, then transfers this policy to tertiary-structure targets to train a general co-design model, and finally applies frontier-guided fine-tuning to refine target-specific trade-offs among secondary-structure fidelity, tertiary-structure fidelity, and sequence diversity. Experiments show that TANGO generates diverse and novel designs, improving tertiary- and secondary-structure performance by 18.3% and 52.7%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.
